justification: Round 2's sole blocking finding was that the 'Best case' bullet's crosslink promised a derivation ('the O(n log n) argument for merge sort') its target (big-o-notation.md#the-pair-search-does-not-have-to-be-quadratic) did not contain -- that section proves a different algorithm (closest-pair search) is O(n log n) by composing a cited Array.Sort bound with a linear scan, and never touches merge sort's own recurrence. The writer retargeted the link to big-o-notation.md#when-the-dropped-constant-decides-the-winner and reworded the sentence. I read that target section directly (not from memory of prior rounds): its second bullet reads 'Merge sort sorts each half recursively and merges the two. Top-down merge sort uses between 1/2 n log2 n and n log2 n comparisons on any input (section 2.2): Theta(n log n) in every case,' immediately preceded by 'Both costs here are from Sedgewick and Wayne, measured in comparisons,' and section 2.2 links to https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/22mergesort/ -- Sedgewick and Wayne's own book site. The anchor 'when-the-dropped-constant-decides-the-winner' resolves to a real H2 heading at that exact slug (verified against the article's own heading text, not just the link syntax). So the target genuinely does state merge sort's Theta(n log n) bound, attributed to Sedgewick and Wayne, exactly as the new anchor text 'merge sort's comparison count' promises -- no more, no less. I then read the reworded sentence in context: '...is the same recurrence merge sort satisfies -- merge sort's own Theta(n log n) bound is asserted with a citation rather than derived from that recurrence (see [merge sort's comparison count](...)), since solving recurrences like this one is left to a future article -- and by the same bound, this recurrence also solves to Theta(n log n).' This no longer claims a derivation exists anywhere; it correctly characterizes the linked section as an assertion-with-citation and explicitly defers recurrence-solving. I checked that 'a future article' is not a fabricated promise: CONTENT_PLAN.md row 89 plans 'analyzing-loops-and-recursion' (pillar Q) with an outline that explicitly includes 'recursion trees -> recurrences and the Master Theorem, three cases with examples' and a figure of 'Recursion tree for T(n)=2T(n/2)+n' -- the same recurrence family. That slug is listed in docs/STATUS.json but no file exists yet at src/content/articles/complexity/analyzing-loops-and-recursion.md, so per the editorial brief's crosslink rule (link only to pages that exist in the build) the writer correctly left this as a bare text reference rather than a hyperlink to a page that doesn't exist -- exactly right, not an oversight. This finding is resolved. On the full fresh read: I independently recomputed, rather than trusted, two of the article's headline numbers. For the average-case double sum at n=8000, sum_{i<j} 2/(j-i+1) evaluates to 121,050.73 (article: '~121,051', 4.17% from the measured 126,318, article says 'within about 4%' -- exact match), versus 2*8000*ln(8000) = 143,795.15 (article: '~143,800', 13.84% off, article says 'about 14% off' -- exact match). For the lopsided-split exercise solution, T(n)=T(n-2)+(n-1) with k=n/2=4000 terms averaging n/2=4000 gives T(8000)=4000^2=16,000,000=n^2/4 exactly, confirming 'a sum of about (n/2)*(n/2) = n^2/4' is self-consistent (this was the round-1 self-contradiction, fixed in round 2 and still correct now). I hand-checked the n(n-1)/2 closed form at both table endpoints (500*499/2=124,750; 8,000*7,999/2=31,996,000) against the printed output blocks -- exact. I re-verified every previously-flagged minor fix is still in place and accurate: the reversed-array split is stated as '(n-1) : 0' (not the old, wrong '0 : n-1'); the duplicates paragraph gives the real per-run counts (2,073/1,942/2,032/1,953) instead of a flat 'repeated 2,000 times each'; and the duplicates-vs-sorted comparison correctly says 'a quarter of sorted's naive worst case of 31,996,000' rather than the old 'barely different'. On this pass I found one new, minor issue the first two rounds did not flag (detailed below): 'under 30 frames at n = 8,000' is not quite accurate against the article's own table, which reports the random-input recursion depth at n=8,000 as exactly 30, not under 30. This is a boundary wording slip, not a substantive error -- the surrounding claim (random depth stays in the tens while sorted depth tracks n exactly) is correct and well-supported by the table. I found no other new problems: every quotation I spot-checked (Sedgewick and Wayne's lightning-strike line, the three-way-partitioning rationale, StackOverflowException's two Learn-page sentences, String.GetHashCode's stability disclaimer, the dotnet/runtime source comment about GetNonRandomizedHashCode, the Crosby/Wallach quote, CVE-2011-3414/MS11-100/December 2011) matches the article's front-matter sources' actual current text, all algorithm costs are stated with their case and condition per the brief's 'every algorithm named gets its cost' rule, and the closing case-summary table is accurate against everything derived above it. run-code.mjs passed twice in this session with identical blocks=17 executed=6. Compared with GeeksforGeeks' Quick Sort Algorithm page, this article remains substantially deeper: exact per-case recurrences, a from-scratch indicator-variable average-case proof cross-checked against a brute-force numerical evaluation, a randomized-pivot fix measured on four input shapes, three-way partitioning for duplicates with a worked exercise, and a real CVE tied to .NET's own per-process hash randomization -- genre-leading content, not merely competent. The one new nit is exactly the kind of thing the rubric's 8.5 anchor ('equal to top-tier quality with only nits') describes, not a blocking defect, so this clears the pass threshold.
